clue.text: Performer caught out at first by microphone

indicators.note: what comes at first in a word is its opening letter
one thing placed by another sits beside it, so the pieces run on side by side

parts.note: c = caught, the cricket scorecard abbreviation
first letter of 'out'
microphone clipped to its first three letters, the everyday short form

explanation.surface: A stand-up act is ambushed by the microphone before the show even starts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Caught out' reads as one phrase, but 'caught' gives C by itself and 'out at first' gives just the O.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: a comic is a comedian, someone who stands on stage telling jokes, and so one kind of entertainer.

clue.text: Coin dispatched to be picked up

indicators.note: a sound is picked up by the ear or a microphone, so the word is heard rather than seen

parts.note: dispatched means posted off; say that word aloud and respell it

explanation.surface: A coin is sent off in the post to be collected at the other end.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Picked up' suggests collecting the coin, but here it means heard: SENT and CENT sound the same.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: the cent is the small copper piece worth one hundredth of a dollar or euro.

clue.text: Note characters turning up during home matches

indicators.note: in a down answer, turning up means reading from the bottom to the top
something that happens during an event sits inside it, so the letters lie within the phrase that follows

parts.note: sitting inside h(OME M)atches

explanation.surface: A note records which players showed up for the home games.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Characters' simply means letters: the answer is made of characters found in 'home matches', read upward.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: a memo, short for memorandum, is a brief written message passed round an office.

clue.text: Cheat with writing one's made to join up

parts.note: to con is to cheat
script = handwriting

explanation.surface: Someone forges documents to get into the army.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a whole phrase describing a person rather than a single word; 'join up' means enlist.
explanation.definitionFit: Descriptive definition: a conscript is drafted into military service by law rather than volunteering.

clue.text: News articles beginning to slate Conservatives

indicators.note: the beginning of a word is its first letter

parts.note: first letter of 'slate'
Tories is the nickname for Britain's Conservative Party

explanation.surface: The papers open by laying into the Conservative government.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Slate' here is British for criticise harshly, which makes the surface a press attack; in the wordplay it only supplies S.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: journalists call each piece they file a story, so the plural covers a paper's reports.

clue.text: Witness was lying about up-and-down affair

parts.note: to witness is to see

indicators.note: something lying about has been turned round, so WAS lies the other way

parts.note: used as it stands, then turned around

explanation.surface: A witness gave false evidence about an on-off relationship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Was lying' looks like perjury, but 'lying about' just flips WAS; 'affair' is not romantic but a thing that goes up and down.
explanation.definitionFit: Descriptive definition: a playground plank pivoting in the middle, each end rising as the other falls.

clue.text: Djokovic, maybe, neither starting nor finishing eggs

indicators.note: a word that neither starts nor finishes has lost its first and last letters

parts.note: Novak Djokovic, the Serbian tennis player; 'maybe' flags that it is one Novak among many
N and K are dropped

explanation.surface: A tennis star neither starts nor finishes his eggs at breakfast.
explanation.walkthrough: The surname points you to the first name: Djokovic is Novak, and only the middle survives.
explanation.definitionFit: Latin plural: ova are egg cells, the word biologists use for the female reproductive cell.

clue.text: Personal letters?

parts.note: the surface reads this as private, but it means belonging to a particular person
not correspondence but characters of the alphabet

explanation.walkthrough: 'Personal letters' sounds like private correspondence; the question mark warns that the letters are alphabet letters belonging to a person.
explanation.definitionFit: Cryptic reading: the capitals that begin your first name and surname are the letters peculiar to you.

clue.text: Scot lacking heart to encourage SNP politician

indicators.note: the heart of a word is its middle, so SCOT loses its central CO

parts.note: SCOT without its middle CO
to urge on is to encourage

explanation.surface: A heartless Scot eggs on a nationalist politician.
explanation.walkthrough: The SNP is the Scottish National Party; Nicola Sturgeon led it and was Scotland's First Minister.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: Nicola Sturgeon led the Scottish National Party from 2014 to 2023.

clue.text: The author's entering one worried candidate

indicators.note: a worried thing is agitated and churned up, so the letters of ONE are jumbled
whatever enters something goes inside it

parts.note: ONE rearranged, split around the insertion
the setter speaking of himself: 'the author's' = mine

explanation.surface: The writer joins a nervous contender in the race.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The author' is the setter, so 'the author's' is the possessive MINE, not I'M.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: someone formally put forward for an election or award is standing as a candidate.

clue.text: Farewell from university following a pass

parts.note: as it stands
to pass away is to die
u = university

explanation.surface: A student says goodbye to university after scraping a pass.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pass' sounds like an exam grade, but it is the verb meaning die.
explanation.definitionFit: Borrowed word: French for 'to God', used in English as a formal goodbye.

clue.text: To start with, scouting contingent walking and climbing

indicators.note: a word's start is its first letter, so take the openings of the next two words

parts.note: first letters of 'scouting' and 'contingent'
rambling = walking in the countryside

explanation.surface: A troop of scouts sets off hiking and clambering over hills.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Walking and climbing' reads as a pair, but only 'walking' is wordplay; 'climbing' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: scrambling is clambering over rough rock using hands as well as feet.

clue.text: Military officer organised air bridge

indicators.note: to organise things is to arrange them into a new order, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: anagram fodder, 9 letters

explanation.surface: An army officer sets up an airlift.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface fits the answer neatly, since organising an air bridge is just the job an officer would do.
explanation.definitionFit: Rank: in the army a brigadier commands a brigade, ranking above colonel.

clue.text: Join RAC finally on roadside?

indicators.note: what comes finally is last, so take the last letter of 'RAC'

parts.note: last letter of RAC
used as it stands
the verge is the grass strip at the side of a road

explanation.surface: Sign up with the RAC, a British motoring breakdown club, once stranded at the roadside.
explanation.walkthrough: The RAC is the Royal Automobile Club, a British breakdown service, which makes the roadside feel natural.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: roads or rivers that converge come together and meet at one point.

clue.text: Agents at ground stand still

indicators.note: the past tense of grind: something ground has been crushed and broken up

parts.note: anagram fodder, 8 letters

explanation.surface: Secret agents at a football ground are told to freeze.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ground' looks like a sports venue, but it is the past tense of grind.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: water that stagnates stops flowing, and an economy that does makes no progress.

clue.text: Get the better of unfashionable humorist

parts.note: out = out of fashion
a wit is a clever, funny person

explanation.surface: Someone scores off a comedian who has gone out of style.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface pits someone against a humorist, and the answer's own second half is that humorist.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: to beat an opponent through cleverness rather than strength.

clue.text: Retreat after retirement to Venetian location

indicators.note: to retire is to draw back, so after retirement the word runs backwards

parts.note: a lair is a hiding place or retreat
used as it stands

explanation.surface: A pensioner withdraws to a spot in Venice.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as moving to Venice after retiring from work; 'retirement' is really the instruction to reverse LAIR.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: a district of Venice by the Grand Canal, famous for its bridge and market.

clue.text: Passionate artist laid up with depression

indicators.note: in a down answer, something laid up is set upward, so it reads from bottom to top

parts.note: RA = Royal Academician, a member of the Royal Academy of Arts
a dent is a hollow or depression

explanation.surface: An emotional painter is bedridden and depressed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Laid up' and 'depression' suggest an ill, gloomy artist; in fact the depression is a hollow in a surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: from Latin for burning, it describes feelings held with fiery enthusiasm.

clue.text: Eating, rave about having no meat

indicators.note: letters turned about have been moved round into a new arrangement

parts.note: anagram fodder, 10 letters

explanation.surface: Someone enthuses about dining without meat.
explanation.walkthrough: The anagram fodder is itself about food, so the whole clue stays on topic.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: a diet or dish free of flesh, fish and fowl is called this.

clue.text: Insult in pub borne by British

indicators.note: in a down answer, what is borne by something is carried on top of it

parts.note: a bar is a pub
b = British

explanation.surface: A British drinker has to put up with an insult in the pub.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Borne by' reads as putting up with the insult; in a down answer it puts BAR above B.
explanation.definitionFit: Figurative: like the hooked point on an arrow, a cutting remark sticks and hurts.

clue.text: Crack shot's first to plug jumbo?

indicators.note: the first of a word is its opening letter

parts.note: a jumbo is a jumbo jet
first letter of 'shot'

explanation.surface: A sharpshooter puts a bullet into an elephant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crack shot' reads as one phrase for a marksman; 'crack' is the definition, a joke, and 'jumbo' is the aircraft, not the elephant.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: a crack, as in wisecrack, is a quick witty remark made for laughs.

clue.text: Come to religious lesson at a church

indicators.note: something at a place is right beside it, so the pieces follow on

parts.note: RE = religious education, a school subject
as it stands
ch = church

explanation.surface: An invitation to come to Sunday school at a church.
explanation.walkthrough: RE is religious education, the name British schools give to lessons about faith.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: travellers who arrive at a destination have got there.

clue.text: Long-handled device regularly used in The Open

indicators.note: things happening regularly come at even intervals, so every other letter is taken

parts.note: t(H)e (O)p(E)n: second, fourth and sixth letters

explanation.surface: A long-handled club gets plenty of use at golf's Open Championship.
explanation.walkthrough: The Open is golf's British Open Championship, so a long-handled device sounds like a putter.
explanation.definitionFit: Descriptive definition: a garden tool with a flat blade on a long shaft, used for weeding.

clue.text: Missing golf, move abroad — somewhere like Dubai?

indicators.note: a word missing a letter has lost it

parts.note: to emigrate is to move abroad
Golf is G in the NATO phonetic alphabet; removed

explanation.surface: Someone relocates overseas to Dubai, giving up their golf.
explanation.walkthrough: Dubai is one of the seven emirates of the United Arab Emirates.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: a state ruled by an emir, and Dubai is one of seven in the UAE.

clue.text: Steelmen starting late forged iron?

indicators.note: a word that starts late has missed its start, so the first letter goes
metal that is forged is hammered into a new shape, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: STEELMEN loses its first letter S

explanation.surface: Steelworkers who clocked on late hammered out some iron.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark shows iron is an example: it is one element among many.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: iron sits in the periodic table, chemical symbol Fe.

clue.text: Argue against Root being withdrawn

indicators.note: something withdrawn is pulled back, so the word reads in reverse

parts.note: a tuber is a swollen root, like a potato

explanation.surface: Someone protests Joe Root, the England cricketer, being taken off.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital R makes Root look like the cricketer, but it is an ordinary root.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: to rebut a claim is to contradict it with evidence or counterargument.
